title: Stocks vs bonds: owning vs lending
summary: See the one difference between a stock and a bond, and why it decides who gets paid and who takes the risk.
objective: Tell whether an investment makes you an owner or a lender, and predict how it behaves when a company does well or badly.

hook.prompt: Ana buys $1,000 of a company's stock. Ben buys $1,000 of the same company's bonds. Next year its profits triple. Who most likely gains more?

options.feedback: Ben's payments were agreed in advance, so bigger profits don't raise them.

options.text: They gain the same, since they each put in $1,000
options.feedback: Same amount in, but stocks and bonds pay out in very different ways.

hook.explanation: Ana owns a slice of the company, so its success is partly hers. Ben lent it money and gets the interest he was promised, no more.

bricks.title: A stock is owning, a bond is lending
bricks.body:
A **stock** (or share) is a small slice of ownership in a company. If the company does well, your slice can rise in value, and it may pay you part of its profits as **dividends**.

A **bond** is a loan. You lend money to a company or a government; it pays you a fixed amount of interest, whatever its profits, and repays the loan on a set date.

term.definition: A loan you make to a company or government, which pays you set interest and repays you on a set date.

visual.html:
Stock

You become an owner

Value rises and falls with the company

Bond

You become a lender

Fixed interest, then your money back
visual.alt: Two cards side by side: Stock, where you become an owner and the value rises and falls with the company, and Bond, where you become a lender and get fixed interest, then your money back.

bricks.prompt: Maya buys a $1,000 bond from her city, paying 4% a year for 10 years. What is she doing?

options.text: Buying a small share of ownership in the city
options.feedback: Ownership slices are stocks, and those come from companies. A bond is a loan, and the city is the borrower.

options.text: Buying a slice of the city's profits
options.feedback: A share of profits comes with owning stock. A bond pays its set 4% whether things go well or not.

bricks.hint: Is Maya becoming an owner, or a lender?
bricks.explanation: Maya lends the city $1,000. It pays her 4% ($40) a year and repays the $1,000 after 10 years.

bricks.prompt: Sort each statement: is it about owning a stock or holding a bond?

items.text: You own a small slice of the company
You're paid a fixed amount of interest
You get your money back on a set date
A government can sell you one
Its value can grow as profits grow

bricks.hint: For each one, ask: does this sound like an owner or a lender?
bricks.explanation: Owners share in the company's ups and downs, through value and dividends. Lenders get set interest and their money back, and governments borrow too.

bricks.title: Lenders get paid first, owners take the risk
bricks.body:
A company must pay its lenders before its owners. Interest is owed on time, and if the company goes bust, its debts are repaid first. Stockholders get whatever is left, often nothing.

So stocks carry more **risk**: their prices swing more, but they have more room to grow. Bonds are steadier and usually grow less over the long run. They're not risk-free: a borrower can still fail to pay.

visual.html:
If a company goes bust, who's repaid?

1stBondholders (lenders)
LastStockholders (owners): whatever is left
visual.alt: A two-step list of who is repaid when a company goes bust: bondholders, the lenders, first; stockholders, the owners, last, getting whatever is left.

bricks.prompt: A company goes bust. After selling everything it owns, it can repay only half of what it borrowed. What do its stockholders get?

options.text: Half their money back, like the lenders
options.feedback: Lenders and owners aren't treated alike. Debts are repaid first, and here the money runs out before the debts are even covered.

options.text: All their money back, because they own the company
options.feedback: Owning comes last in line, not first. Owners share the losses, not just the gains.

bricks.hint: Who is repaid first, and is there anything left after them?
bricks.explanation: Lenders are repaid first, and they only get half. Nothing is left over, so the owners' stock is worth nothing.

options.feedback: B climbs slowly and smoothly. That steady path fits bonds, which pay fixed interest.

options.text: Neither: stocks always grow faster, with no drops
options.feedback: Stocks grow more over the long run, but their prices swing on the way, including drops.

bricks.hint: Which kind of investment swings more, and which usually grows more over time?
bricks.explanation: Line A swings up and down, even dropping below where it started, yet ends higher. That's the typical stock pattern: more risk, more room to grow.

challenge.prompt: GreenPower sells both stock and bonds. One year its profits fall sharply, but it stays in business and pays its bills. Which are likely?

options.text: Its bondholders still get their usual interest
Its bondholders' interest is cut to match the lower profits
options.feedback: Bond interest is fixed, whatever the profits. As long as the company pays its bills, lenders get the agreed amount.

options.text: Its stockholders are protected because owners are paid first
options.feedback: It's the other way around: lenders are paid first. Owners take the hit when the company does badly.

challenge.hint: Think about each group separately: what were lenders promised, and what do owners share in?
challenge.explanation: Lenders were promised fixed interest, and the company can still pay it. Owners share in the company's fortunes, so falling profits usually pull the stock price down.

takeaways: A stock makes you a part-owner of a company; a bond makes you a lender to a company or government.
Bondholders get fixed interest and are repaid first; stockholders get whatever is left.
Stocks swing more but have more room to grow; bonds are steadier and usually grow less.
